fact: A giraffe's tongue can be around 45 to 50 centimetres long, and it is dark in colour.
Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs. Only the platypus and the echidnas do this.
African elephants are the largest animals walking the Earth.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal. It can reach speeds of up to about 114 km/h.
Under its thick white-looking fur, a polar bear has black skin.
Algae grow in a sloth's fur, giving it a green tint that helps it blend in with the trees.
Male humpback whales sing complex songs during the breeding season.
source_org: NOAA Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary

fact: An adult hedgehog has between 5,000 and 7,000 spines, which are made of keratin.
Bamboo makes up about 99% of a giant panda's diet, and a panda can eat 12 to 38 kg of it every day.
A tiger's skin is striped as well as its fur.
A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean. It crawls into its mother's pouch to keep growing.
Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, which are made of keratin like your fingernails.
The capybara is the largest rodent in the world.
Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open shellfish such as clams and sea urchins.
A camel's hump stores fat, not water. The fat can be used for energy when food is scarce.
A dog's nose has up to 300 million smell receptors. A human nose has about 6 million.
Despite its zebra-like stripes, the okapi's closest living relative is the giraffe.
The name aardvark means "earth pig" in Afrikaans. Aardvarks dig up ants and termites to eat.
Flying foxes find fruit and nectar using their excellent eyesight and sense of smell. They do not use echolocation.
Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" to tell other bees in the hive which direction and how far to fly to find food.
Monarch butterflies in North America migrate up to about 3,000 miles (4,800 km) to spend the winter in Mexico and California.
Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry. They use them to grow a fungus garden, which feeds their young.
source_org: McGill University Office for Science and Society

fact: A ladybird's bright colours warn predators that it tastes bad, and it can ooze a bitter, smelly fluid from its leg joints.
A glow-worm is not a worm but a beetle. The wingless females glow at night to attract flying males.
Adult atlas moths have no mouths, so they never eat or drink.
Male Hercules beetles can measure up to about 17 centimetres long, making them among the largest flying insects.
Indian stick insects are all female. They lay eggs that hatch without any males.
A praying mantis can turn its head about 180 degrees to look over its shoulder.
A desert locust swarm can contain millions of insects and can travel 130 to 150 kilometres or more in a day.
source_org: Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN

fact: Male mosquitoes do not bite. Most female mosquitoes need a blood meal before they can produce eggs.
source_org: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

fact: Some dung beetles use the light of the Milky Way to roll their dung balls in a straight line at night.
Periodical cicadas live underground as nymphs for 13 or 17 years, then come out together in huge numbers.
Bumblebees can shake pollen out of flowers such as tomatoes by vibrating their flight muscles. This is called buzz pollination.
A single silkworm cocoon is made from one silk filament that can be 600 to 1,500 metres long.
source_org: Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN

fact: Weaver ants build nests by pulling leaves together and gluing them with silk made by their own larvae.
The hummingbird hawk-moth hovers in front of flowers and drinks nectar through its long tongue, just like a hummingbird.
A giant wētā from New Zealand holds the record for the heaviest insect ever weighed: 71 grams.
Female earwigs are caring mothers. They guard and clean their eggs and look after the young nymphs.
source_org: Clemson University Home & Garden Information Center

fact: Stag beetle larvae live in rotting wood for several years, sometimes up to seven, before turning into adults.
When diving after prey, a peregrine falcon can reach about 320 km/h, the fastest dive of any bird.
Male emperor penguins balance their egg on their feet for 65 to 75 days through the Antarctic winter.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
source_org: UC Davis Hummingbird Health and Conservation Program

fact: A barn owl's hearing is so good that it can find and catch prey in complete darkness.
The ostrich is the largest living bird and lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
Flamingos are pink because of natural colours called carotenoids in the algae and shrimps they eat.
Engineers redesigned the nose of a Japanese bullet train to copy the shape of a kingfisher's beak, making it quieter and faster.
A woodpecker's long tongue wraps around the back of its skull when it is pulled in.
Both male and female robins sing in winter to defend their own territories.
Swallows that nest in the UK fly all the way to Africa for the winter, then return in spring.
A puffin can hold ten or more small fish in its beak at once, using its spiny tongue to keep them in place.
The kākāpō of New Zealand is the world's heaviest parrot. It cannot fly and is active at night.
A shoebill can stand completely still for a long time in a swamp, waiting to grab fish such as lungfish with its huge bill.
Young hoatzins have claws on their wings, which they use to clamber back up the tree to their nest.
The secretary bird kills snakes with powerful, lightning-fast kicks.
The superb lyrebird is a brilliant mimic. It can copy the songs of many other birds and other sounds it hears.
Only male peafowl, called peacocks, have the long, colourful train. Females are called peahens.
Male Andean condors have been reported with wingspans of up to 3.2 metres.
Cassowaries swallow rainforest fruits whole and spread the seeds in their droppings, helping new trees to grow.
Unlike most owls, snowy owls often hunt in daylight, which helps during the long days of the Arctic summer.
source_org: Cornell Lab of Ornithology (All About Birds)

fact: A chameleon can move each eye on its own, so it can look in two different directions at the same time.
Komodo dragons are among the largest and heaviest lizards on Earth. The largest one measured was over 3 metres long.
The tuatara is not a lizard. It is the only living member of an ancient group of reptiles that first appeared over 200 million years ago.
Galápagos giant tortoises can live for more than 100 years.
The green sea turtle is named after the greenish colour of its fat, which comes from the seagrass and algae it eats.
The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake. It can grow to more than 5 metres long.
The thorny devil can drink through its skin. Tiny channels in its skin carry water up to its mouth.
The marine iguana is the only lizard that feeds in the sea. It sneezes out the extra salt it swallows.
Geckos can climb walls because their toes are covered in millions of tiny hairs that cling to surfaces.
A young basilisk lizard can run across the surface of water on its back legs for a short distance.
When threatened, the frilled lizard opens a large frill of skin around its neck, hisses and gapes its mouth to scare predators.
Leatherbacks are the largest turtles and can dive more than 1,000 metres deep.
The slow worm is not a worm or a snake. It is a legless lizard that can blink its eyelids, which snakes cannot do.
A substance found in Gila monster saliva led scientists to develop a medicine for people with type 2 diabetes.
The black mamba is usually grey or brown. It is named after the inky black colour inside its mouth.
The alligator snapping turtle has a bright red, worm-shaped lure on its tongue that tricks fish into swimming close.
The adder is Britain's only venomous snake. It is shy and usually moves away from people.
The temperature of an alligator's nest decides whether the eggs hatch as males or females.
When in danger, a grass snake often plays dead.
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
An axolotl can regrow lost limbs and even some of its organs.
Cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to eat beetles on sugar cane farms, but they spread widely and became a serious pest.
The golden poison frog is far more deadly than any other poison frog. Wild frogs get their poison from the insects they eat.
Some glass frogs have see-through bellies, so you can see their heart and other organs.
In winter, a wood frog can freeze almost solid. Its heart stops beating, then it thaws out and hops away in spring.
source_org: US National Park Service (Gates of the Arctic)

fact: The olm is a blind salamander that lives in dark caves. Scientists think it can live past 100 years.
Male Darwin's frogs keep their tadpoles inside their vocal sac until they turn into tiny froglets.
Surinam toad eggs sink into the skin on the mother's back, and fully formed baby toads later pop out.
Caecilians are amphibians with no legs. They look like large worms and most live underground.
Many frogs do not drink with their mouths. They soak up water through a special 'drinking patch' of skin.
In England the great crested newt is a protected species, so harming newts or damaging their ponds is against the law.
The fire salamander's bright yellow and black colours warn predators that its skin produces poison.
Giant salamanders from China are the largest amphibians in the world. The biggest reported was about 1.75 metres long.
The goliath frog of West Africa is the largest frog in the world. It can weigh 3 kilograms or more.
Tiny green algae live inside spotted salamander eggs and even inside the cells of the growing embryos.
When a red-eyed tree frog is disturbed, it suddenly opens its bright red eyes, which can startle a predator.
The purple frog of India lives underground and comes to the surface for just a few days each year, at the start of the monsoon, to breed.
source_org: EDGE of Existence (Zoological Society of London)

fact: From the 1930s to the 1960s, African clawed frogs were used in hospitals as an early pregnancy test.
The mudpuppy keeps its bushy red gills for its whole life and never leaves the water.
The hellbender takes in most of its oxygen through the wrinkly folds of skin along its body.
